title: Job 19:13–22
context: Job continues. He describes his estrangement from brothers, relatives, household, servants, wife, children, and close friends, and his physical wasting (19:13–20), then pleads with his friends for pity rather than pursuit (19:21–22).

verses.text: “He has put my brothers far from me. My acquaintances are wholly estranged from me.
verses.arminianNotes: “He has put my brothers far from me. My acquaintances are wholly estranged from me.” Arminian readers see Job grieving social isolation as part of his affliction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the pain of estrangement. Job attributes even his loneliness to God’s hand, and readers in this tradition see the depth of his sense of abandonment.

verses.text: My relatives have gone away. My familiar friends have forgotten me.
verses.arminianNotes: “My relatives have gone away. My familiar friends have forgotten me.” Arminian readers see the loss of the support that family and friends should provide in suffering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a lament over forsaken relationships. Readers in this tradition take it as a call for the community of faith to stay near those who suffer rather than withdraw.

verses.text: Those who dwell in my house and my maids consider me a stranger. I am an alien in their sight.
verses.arminianNotes: “Those who dwell in my house and my maids consider me a stranger.” Arminian readers see Job’s reversal of status, now treated as an outsider in his own household.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a household turned against its master. Readers in this tradition note how suffering can bring social humiliation as well as bodily pain.

verses.text: I call to my servant, and he gives me no answer. I beg him with my mouth.
verses.arminianNotes: “I call to my servant, and he gives me no answer. I beg him with my mouth.” Arminian readers see the humiliation of a once-respected man who must plead with his own servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a painful reversal of roles. Readers in this tradition note the contrast with Job’s former honor, which he will recall in chapter 29.

verses.text: My breath is offensive to my wife. I am loathsome to the children of my own mother.
verses.arminianNotes: “My breath is offensive to my wife. I am loathsome to the children of my own mother.” Arminian readers see the effects of Job’s illness isolating him even from those closest to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the cost of Job’s disease in his closest relationships. Readers in this tradition read the line with compassion and avoid speculating beyond what the text says.

verses.text: Even young children despise me. If I arise, they speak against me.
verses.arminianNotes: “Even young children despise me. If I arise, they speak against me.” Arminian readers see the depth of Job’s disgrace in a culture that expected the young to honor elders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a sign of complete loss of standing. Readers in this tradition note how Job’s suffering has inverted the respect he once received from all ages.

verses.text: All my familiar friends abhor me. They whom I loved have turned against me.
verses.arminianNotes: “All my familiar friends abhor me. They whom I loved have turned against me.” Arminian readers see betrayal by those Job loved, perhaps including the friends who now accuse him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the pain of love unreturned. Readers in this tradition note that the verse may include the three friends, whose speeches have added to Job’s isolation.

verses.text: My bones stick to my skin and to my flesh. I have escaped by the skin of my teeth.
verses.arminianNotes: “My bones stick to my skin and to my flesh. I have escaped by the skin of my teeth.” Arminian readers see Job’s physical wasting and his sense of barely surviving.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a picture of extreme weakness. The phrase “the skin of my teeth” is obscure in its exact sense, but readers in this tradition commonly take it to mean narrow escape.

verses.text: “Have pity on me. Have pity on me, you my friends, for the hand of God has touched me.
verses.arminianNotes: “Have pity on me. Have pity on me, you my friends, for the hand of God has touched me.” Arminian readers see Job pleading for compassion instead of argument.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a plea for mercy from friends. Readers in this tradition take the verse as a pastoral lesson that sufferers first need pity, not explanations.

verses.text: Why do you persecute me as God, and are not satisfied with my flesh?
verses.arminianNotes: “Why do you persecute me as God, and are not satisfied with my flesh?” Arminian readers see Job accusing his friends of adding to his suffering as if they shared God’s role.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Job protesting the friends’ presumption. Readers in this tradition note that the friends act as judges, a role Job believes belongs to God alone.
